stemMd: The passage suggests that the most consequential effect of the reading rooms was
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: the replacement of reading aloud by silent reading within the household.

options.label: B
options.textMd: the growth of a readership large enough to sustain the cheap newspapers that followed.

options.label: C
options.textMd: the political radicalisation of the shopkeepers and clerks who subscribed.

options.label: D
options.textMd: a habit of setting rival accounts of an event side by side and noticing where they differ.

explanationMd:
The third paragraph tells you where to look. It reports what historians have emphasised, then turns: "But the more consequential change may have been the quieter one." Whatever follows that sentence is the passage's own candidate.

What follows is that a subscriber could not answer an author, only turn to a rival account — and so "the habit of comparison — of holding one account of an event beside another and noticing the distance between them — is a habit the rooms taught almost accidentally." The final paragraph then confirms the choice by saying that this habit "outlived the institution". Option A is that habit.

**How to check.** A passage that contrasts a received view with its own will usually restate its own view at the end, in different words. Here the last sentence — what was learned was "not how to read a particular periodical but how to distrust one" — is the habit of comparison described from the reader's side. An option consistent with both paragraph three's turn and paragraph four's closing line is the passage's view; an option consistent with only one of them is not.

distractorRationale.c: Political argument is the reading the passage attributes to *historians* before setting it aside as the less consequential change. The option is not absurd, but it names the view the passage explicitly declines to endorse as the most important one.
distractorRationale.a: The first paragraph describes reading aloud as the earlier norm, but the passage never claims the rooms ended it in the household; it says the rooms changed the arithmetic 'without, at first, changing its manners'. This option turns background scene-setting into an asserted effect.
distractorRationale.b: The passage mentions cheap newspapers only as a force that later undercut the rooms, in the fourth paragraph. This option reverses the direction of that relation, making the rooms the cause of what the passage presents as their competitor.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying history passage on eighteenth-century subscription reading rooms, asking what the passage suggests was the rooms' most consequential effect.

independentSolve.workingNotes: 'But the more consequential change may have been the quieter one... The habit of comparison — of holding one account of an event beside another and noticing the distance between them.' C is the historians' view the passage downgrades; A and B are never claimed.

review.notes: Author's working: paragraph 3 marks the passage's own candidate with 'the more consequential change may have been the quieter one' and identifies it as the habit of comparison, which paragraph 4 says outlived the institution. Option A matches. B is the historians' view the passage subordinates, C overreads paragraph 1, D reverses the causal relation stated in paragraph 4.
